passage: The support queue in the Hyderabad office blinked red: twelve tickets waiting. Elizabeth, in her second week, turned from her screen. "Kiran, the refund won't go through. It keeps saying 'invalid code'." Kiran's fingers itched; he could fix it in thirty seconds. He pulled a chair over instead. "What have you tried so far?" "Re-entering the amount. Refreshing the page." "Good. One hint: look at the date on the order." Elizabeth scrolled. "Oh. It's older than ninety days. So it needs the manual form?" "Where would you find that?" She found it in the shared folder, filled it in and sent it. It took her seven minutes. Their team lead raised an eyebrow at the growing queue. Kiran shrugged. By Friday Elizabeth was clearing refund tickets faster than he did.

qa.q: How many tickets were waiting in the support queue?
qa.a: Twelve tickets.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when Elizabeth asked for help, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt impatient to fix it himself in thirty seconds; the passage says his fingers itched.

qa.q: Why was asking 'What have you tried so far?' a good first move?
qa.a: It showed Kiran what Elizabeth already knew, so the single hint about the date could land exactly where she was stuck.

qa.q: How might the team lead see those seven minutes differently by Friday?
qa.a: The team lead first frowned at the growing queue, but by Friday could see Elizabeth clearing refund tickets faster than Kiran, so the slow start paid off.

grounding: A junior employee coaching a new hire asks what she has tried, gives one hint and lets her finish, accepting a slower queue that builds a capable colleague.

passage: "Zainab, the totals don't match. I've been at it an hour." Zainab rolled her chair over. "Show me. What have you checked?" "Every row, twice. The formula's the same as yours." "Okay. One thing: are any of the dates stored as text?" Aditi frowned. "How would I know?" "What happens when you sort them?" Aditi sorted. Four rows jumped to the bottom. "Those four! They didn't count." "So what now?" "Convert them... and run the totals again?" "Try it." Zainab's phone buzzed: the client wanted the file by five. It was ten past four. She kept her hands in her lap. Aditi fixed the four rows by four thirty-two. "It matches!" "Next month you'll teach the new joiner that trick," Zainab said.

qa.q: How many rows jumped to the bottom when Aditi sorted the dates?
qa.a: Four rows.

qa.q: What was Zainab likely feeling when the client's message buzzed, and what did she do with it?
qa.a: She likely felt the pressure of the five o'clock deadline, but she kept her hands in her lap and let Aditi finish.

qa.q: Which choice by Zainab made the fix Aditi's own?
qa.a: She asked what Aditi had checked, gave one hint about dates stored as text, then let Aditi sort, spot and fix the rows.

qa.q: What is it like for Aditi to find the four rows without being shown?
qa.a: Aditi gets the thrill of solving it after an hour of frustration, and learns a trick worth passing on to the next joiner.

grounding: A young accountant coaching a new colleague asks what was tried, offers one hint and resists taking over despite a deadline.

passage: My name is Nitin, and I've been a sous-chef for two years. When Hafsa joined our kitchen last spring, my first instinct was to grab the pan from her every time the sauce split. It would have saved four minutes in a Friday rush. I did it once. She watched, nodded, and the next night split the sauce again, the same way. So I changed. When it split, I asked, "What did you do just before?" She said she'd turned the heat up to hurry. "One tip: take it off the flame and whisk in a spoon of cold water." Then I stepped back, even with tickets piling up. The head chef grumbled. Hafsa rescued it herself, slowly. Six months on, she's training our newest cook, and she does it the same way: asks first, one hint, hands off.

qa.q: What did Hafsa say she had done just before the sauce split?
qa.a: She'd turned the heat up to hurry.

qa.q: Why did Nitin decide to change after Hafsa split the sauce the same way again?
qa.a: Nitin realised grabbing the pan had taught her nothing; it saved time that night but left her just as stuck.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Nitin coached Hafsa?
qa.a: Asking what she did just before, giving one tip and stepping back despite the tickets, which let her rescue the sauce herself.

qa.q: How might the head chef see Nitin's slower way six months later?
qa.a: The head chef grumbled at first, but now that Hafsa is training the newest cook, the lost minutes may look well spent.

grounding: A young sous-chef stops taking over, asks what a new cook did, offers one tip and lets her finish, which builds a colleague who now trains others.

passage:
Floor supervisor's note, cutting section, 9 February. Written by Kavitha.
Tenzin joined us on Monday, and Nirmala, twenty-four, has been teaching Tenzin pattern grading. Today the export order was due by four, and Tenzin's extra-large sleeve came out too narrow. I watched Nirmala's hand move toward the scissors, then stop. She asked, "What have you checked so far?" Tenzin listed the chest and the length. Nirmala gave one hint: "Check which line you moved the grade from." Then she went back to her own table.
It took Tenzin twenty minutes. Nirmala could have fixed it in five, and the order left at ten to four instead of three. But by evening Tenzin graded the collar alone.
Next: pair them again for the March order, and ask Nirmala to lead the new-hire session.

qa.q: By what time was the export order due?
qa.a: The export order was due by four.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's hand stopping near the scissors suggest she felt?
qa.a: She was tempted to take over for speed, but held back, trusting that Tenzin needed to finish the fix.

qa.q: What did Nirmala's slower route cost, and what did it buy?
qa.a: The order left close to four instead of three, but by evening Tenzin graded the collar alone, so the section gained a capable colleague.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tenzin to be asked 'What have you checked so far?' instead of being handed a fixed sleeve?
qa.a: Tenzin's work is taken seriously; it may feel slower and tense, but finding the mistake builds real confidence.

grounding: A supervisor records a junior cutter asking a new hire what was tried, giving one hint and letting the new hire finish despite the deadline.

passage:
Wed, 11 pm
Jatin's first week at the station. Tonight he had to cut a ten-minute interview into a three-minute clip for the morning show, and I could have done it in fifteen minutes. My fingers actually hovered over his keyboard.
Instead I asked what he'd tried. He'd cut from the start and run out of time before the good part. One hint: find the best thirty seconds first, then build around it. Then I made myself go and refill the water jug.
He took nearly an hour. We missed the eleven o'clock handover, and the producer gave me a look.
But the clip was good. Better than mine would have been, honestly, because he kept the bit where the fisherman laughs.
Next week he'll do it in twenty minutes, and I'll have a colleague, not a trainee. Worth one look from the producer.
Amandeep

qa.q: What hint did Amandeep give Jatin?
qa.a: Find the best thirty seconds first, then build around it.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep go and refill the water jug?
qa.a: Amandeep wanted to get away from the urge to take over, so that Jatin would finish the clip alone.

qa.q: Was the slower route worth the missed handover, and why?
qa.a: Yes: the producer's look cost little, while Jatin made a better clip and will soon be a colleague who can do it fast.

qa.q: How might the producer have seen the missed handover differently from Amandeep?
qa.a: The producer probably saw only a delay, not the training that Amandeep was putting in for next week's shows.

grounding: A station worker coaching a new hire asks what he tried, gives one hint and resists taking over, accepting a slower night for a more capable colleague.
